units.title: CART: split objectives, impurity, stopping and pruning
outcomes: Compute weighted Gini, entropy and variance reduction for a candidate split by hand and name the winning split.
Implement a CART-style best-split scan with a stated tie rule, stopping conditions and leaf predictions, and differential-test it against sklearn on small data.
Predict how max_depth, min_samples_split and ccp_alpha change bias, variance and tree size.
units.why: Trees decide by recursive splits, so every later ensemble inherits their split logic, their variance and their failure modes. If you cannot score a split by hand, forest and boosting diagnostics stay magic.

study.title: ISLP Chapter 8: regression and classification trees
study.locator: Sections 8.1.1 and 8.1.2 (pp. 331 to 339): recursive binary splitting, Gini versus entropy similarity, and classification error reserved for pruning

focus: Split quality is the weighted child impurity G = (nL/n) H(L) + (nR/n) H(R). The parent impurity never enters except through the choice of H.

sklearn tries midpoints between sorted distinct values with greedy exhaustive search, while Deep-ML 138 scores the raw values: the same four points yield threshold 3.0 under sklearn and 2.5 in problem 138.
Gini and entropy are numerically close and either works for growing; ISLP reserves the classification error rate for pruning toward accuracy.
ccp_alpha penalizes leaf count and prunes the weakest link first, which produces the nested candidate path that cross-validation then selects from.
units.reproduce: By hand on ordered labels A, B, A, A, A: parent Gini 0.32, split after the 2nd instance gives 2/5 times 0.5 + 3/5 times 0 = 0.2, split after the 1st gives 0.3. Then implement a midpoint scan with first-in-scan tie wins and match sklearn threshold 1.5 on X = [0, 1, 2, 3] with y = [0, 0, 1, 1] at max_depth = 1.
traps: Equal impurity does not mean a unique split. Identical features resolve to feature 1 under seeds 0 and 1 but feature 0 under seed 42, so your scanner must define first-wins and test it.
A child can be less pure than its parent: the A, B child has Gini 0.5 against the parent 0.32. Only the weighted sum has to decrease.
HoML Chapter 5 never sets criterion, so every tree there is Gini. Request entropy explicitly, and remember the 138-versus-sklearn threshold convention before comparing answers.

selfTest.q: A node holds 3 positives and 1 negative. What are its Gini impurity and its entropy in bits?
Why does ISLP call the error rate weak for growing but prefer it for pruning?
selfTest.a: Growing needs sensitivity to purity shifts that leave the majority label unchanged. Pruning selects the final tree for accuracy, which is exactly what the error rate measures.

selfTest.q: The same data and code give different trees under a new random_state. Is that a bug?
selfTest.a: No. Tied splits can resolve differently across seeds, as the identical-feature test shows. Fix the seed for reproducibility and define your own deterministic tie rule.

selfTest.q: One leaf holds one vote for each of three classes. What does sklearn predict and with what probabilities?
selfTest.a: It predicts classes_[0], the lowest index, with probabilities [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]. Argmax takes the first maximum.

units.title: Bagging, random forests and out-of-bag estimates
outcomes: Explain why bagging cuts variance for deep trees and why the error stabilizes as the tree count grows instead of overfitting.
Explain how random feature subsets decorrelate trees and how max_features trades correlation against strength.
Measure out-of-bag error against held-out error and read n_estimators, max_features and oob_score settings in sklearn.
units.why: Single trees have high variance: the same algorithm learns visibly different models from the same data. Bagging plus feature subsampling is the standard fix, and out-of-bag scoring gives a nearly free error estimate.

study.title: sklearn bagging meta-estimator
study.locator: 1.11.3 Bagging: bootstrap versus pasting, max_samples, max_features and oob_score

focus: A bootstrap covers about 63.2 percent of unique points since (1 - 1/n)^n tends to 1/e. Each point is predicted by the trees that missed it, and the moons check gives OOB 0.934 against held-out 0.932.
Bagging helps unstable learners because averaging kills variance while bias stays put. Adding trees stabilizes the error; unlike boosting it has no residual-chasing loop to overfit with.
Forests force different top splits by sampling m near sqrt(p) predictors per split, which decorrelates trees that would otherwise copy one strong predictor.
sklearn defaults differ by task: the regressor uses max_features 1.0, which is plain bagging, and ExtraTrees uses bootstrap False with random splits.
units.reproduce: Derive P(missed) = (1 - 1/n)^n tending to 1/e near 0.368, simulate n = 1000 to see about 63.4 percent unique, then fit RandomForestClassifier with 200 trees and oob_score True on the moons split and show OOB 0.934 against held-out 0.932.
traps: OOB rides along with the final fit and reads pessimistic, so use it for monitoring and keep cross-validation for selection.
Soft voting needs predict_proba from every member. A default SVC in sklearn 1.9 has none, so a soft voter mixing one fails loudly.
Assuming sqrt features for a regressor silently turns the forest into bagging. Read max_features per estimator instead of quoting the classifier rule.

selfTest.q: From n = 200 points, how many land out of bag and how many trees predict each one?
selfTest.a: About 0.368 times 200 = 74 points are missed per tree, and each point is predicted by the roughly B/3 trees whose samples skipped it.

selfTest.q: Ten bagged trees give red probabilities 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.2, 0.55, 0.6, 0.6, 0.65, 0.7 and 0.75. What do majority vote and probability averaging predict?
selfTest.a: Majority vote says red with 6 of 10 above 0.5. Averaging gives 0.45 and says green. The combination rule changes the answer.

selfTest.q: Is a default RandomForestRegressor closer to a sqrt forest or to bagged trees?
selfTest.a: Bagged trees, because its max_features default is 1.0. The sqrt default applies to classifiers only.

selfTest.q: Why does raising B not overfit bagging while it can overfit boosting?
selfTest.a: Bagging averages fixed-complexity trees fit on resamples, so variance shrinks and bias holds. Boosting keeps fitting residuals, so late trees can chase noise; choose B by validation.

units.title: AdaBoost and gradient boosting
outcomes: Derive the AdaBoost reweighting step of error rate, learner weight and distribution update, and run one round by hand.
Derive pseudo-residual fitting for squared and logistic loss and explain shrinkage, interaction depth and early stopping.
Implement stage-wise boosting around stumps, match sklearn on a toy, and diagnose noise sensitivity and overfitting by iteration count.
units.why: Boosting turns weak rules into strong models by fitting what is left over. The same loop powers the gradient boosting libraries, so its failure modes of noise chasing and late overfitting follow you into production.

next.note: Configure the production implementations of this loop.
Attribute the boosted model without fooling yourself.

study.locator: Section 8.2.3 with Algorithm 8.2 and the three tuning parameters B, shrinkage lambda and interaction depth d (pp. 347 to 349)

study.title: sklearn gradient boosting: loss, shrinkage and subsampling
study.locator: 1.11.1.2.5 Shrinkage via learning rate (learning_rate at or below 0.1 with large n_estimators) and 1.11.1.2.6 Subsampling (subsample 0.5, OOB pessimistic so prefer cross-validation)

focus: AdaBoost scores the round by the weighted error r, pays the learner alpha = learning_rate times ln((1 - r)/r), multiplies wrong-point weights by exp(alpha) and renormalizes. The hand round gives r = 0.25, alpha = 0.5493 and weights [0.2113, 0.2113, 0.366, 0.2113], matching estimator_weights_.

Gradient boosting fits each tree to pseudo-residuals, the negative gradients of the loss. For squared loss those are ordinary residuals, and mean plus a depth-2 stump on residuals exactly equals a one-tree GBM.
Shrinkage, depth and count interact: small lambda needs large B with typical values 0.01 or 0.001, depth-1 stumps give additive single-variable terms, and subsample 0.5 adds bagging noise.
Boosting uses no bootstrap and each tree depends on its predecessors, so B is a genuine overfitting knob. Choose it by validation or early stopping, unlike bagging counts.
units.reproduce: Run one AdaBoost round by hand on X = [0, 1, 2, 3] with y = [0, 1, 0, 1] and learning_rate 0.5: stump threshold 0.5, r = 0.25, alpha = 0.5493, new weights [0.2113, 0.2113, 0.366, 0.2113]. Confirm alpha against AdaBoostClassifier estimator_weights_. Then show GradientBoostingRegressor with squared loss, learning_rate 1.0 and one depth-2 tree equals the target mean plus a depth-2 stump fit on residuals, on 50 sine points with noise 0.05 at seed 0.
traps: Copying algorithm='SAMME' from the notebook raises TypeError in sklearn 1.9. The parameter is gone and discrete SAMME is the only behavior.
AdaBoost pushes weight exponentially onto mistakes, so mislabeled points attract ever more attention. Noisy labels hurt it more than they hurt bagging.
The learning_rate 1.0 residual demo is didactic. Real runs shrink to 0.1 or below with many more trees, or the residual fit jumps past good solutions.

selfTest.q: A stump has weighted error 0.25 with learning_rate 0.5. What learner weight does AdaBoost assign, and what happens to a wrong point starting at 0.25?
selfTest.a: alpha = 0.5 ln(3) = 0.5493. The wrong point goes to 0.25 times exp(0.5493) = 0.433 before renormalization, which is 0.366 after.

selfTest.q: Why does boosting depth-1 stumps produce an additive model?
selfTest.a: Each stump splits on one variable, so each term is a function of one variable only. The sum over rounds is a sum of single-variable terms.

selfTest.q: A GBM with 5000 trees, learning_rate 0.5 and no validation set scores perfectly in training but poorly on new data. What broke and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: Late trees overfit the residuals. Shrink the learning rate toward 0.1 or below, add row or column subsampling, and pick the iteration count by early stopping on validation.

selfTest.q: How does boosting reuse data differently from bagging?
selfTest.a: Bagging fits independent trees on bootstrap copies. Boosting refits the same data with modified weights or residuals, so each tree depends strongly on the ones before it.

study.locator: Cells around HistGradientBoostingRegressor with categorical_features=[0]: binned training with a native categorical slot

focus: Learn the name map: step size is eta, learning_rate or shrinkage_rate; rows are subsample, bagging_fraction or subsample; columns are colsample_bytree, feature_fraction or rsm; L2 is lambda, lambda_l2 or l2_leaf_reg.

Defaults that bite: XGBoost eta 0.3 against 0.1 and 0.03 elsewhere, CatBoost iterations 1000 with automatic learning rate, LightGBM bagging off until bagging_freq passes 0, LightGBM leaves growing leaf-wise to num_leaves 31 regardless of max_depth -1, CatBoost symmetric trees at depth 6.

Early stopping differs per library: XGBoost takes early_stopping_rounds with eval_set and predicts from the best iteration, LightGBM takes a callback, CatBoost takes eval_set with use_best_model, HGBT stops by itself on large data.

Categorical handling differs too: CatBoost takes raw categories with ordered statistics and one-hot only below one_hot_max_size 2, LightGBM takes integer-coded categorical features, XGBoost expects encoded input.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the 200-round learning-rate 0.05 depth-4 row and column 0.8 L2 1.0 early-stopped configuration for all four libraries, then correct every name and default against the docs. Run the HGBT version with max_iter 200, learning_rate 0.05, max_depth 4, l2_regularization 1.0 and early stopping on the moons split at seed 0, and report n_iter_ 200 with train accuracy 0.955 as in the reference run under sklearn 1.9.1.
traps: num_leaves 31 with max_depth 4 cannot grow 31 leaves: depth caps the tree at 16 leaves, so set both consistently instead of copying the default.
bagging_fraction 0.8 alone changes nothing in LightGBM. Bagging stays off until bagging_freq is set above 0.
Copying n_estimators 100 into CatBoost without setting the learning rate silently swaps the shrinkage regime, since CatBoost defaults to 1000 iterations with an automatic rate.

selfTest.q: What are the default step sizes in XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost?
selfTest.a: XGBoost eta 0.3, LightGBM learning_rate 0.1, CatBoost learning_rate 0.03 with automatic tuning for Logloss, MultiClass and RMSE.

selfTest.q: Name the row-sampling parameter in each of the three libraries and any enabling switch.
selfTest.a: XGBoost subsample, LightGBM bagging_fraction which needs bagging_freq above 0, CatBoost subsample under its bootstrap type with MVS 0.8 on CPU.

selfTest.q: Should low-cardinality string columns be one-hot encoded for CatBoost?
selfTest.a: No. Pass them as categorical features and let ordered target statistics handle them; one-hot applies only below one_hot_max_size, default 2.

selfTest.q: When does sklearn HGBT stop early without an explicit validation set?
selfTest.a: With early_stopping auto, which is the default, it reserves validation internally on data above 10000 rows. Smaller data runs the full max_iter unless validation is passed.
